en: It establishes positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
because the negation of a negation is of the nature of an affirmation.
If it is argued that there is no absence from non-existent similar instances (*asapakṣa*) because such a non-similar instance (*asapakṣa*) does not exist at all;
"No"—this very [negation] is the cessation of cessation; for how could that which is non-existent be desired?
For even when non-existent, there exists the negation of a non-entity, which is itself an entity.

But since the negation of an existent entity is not possible, the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya), whose wisdom is unerring, does not accept a negation directed toward that [existent], yet he employs the conventional expression "non-existence" for what is non-existent. And this point has been thoroughly examined under the heading: "When there is no [existent], there is no non-existence."

3: This is another point; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here. Furthermore, the self cannot be considered doubtful simply because it is non-existent, since that would contradict the very operation of the means of proving existence.
And it was not approached by another in that manner.

It is not so, because it follows from what is accepted [by the opponent] without valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*), which leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it is not logical to establish the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) by the force of mere acceptance and then proceed with the application of valid means of cognition.
For in this way, the self would be established by scripture (āgama),
not established by inference (anumāna);
therefore, it would exist even in the absence of any distinction [from the body].
The exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa) would be doubtful in the case of [the reasons] such as "possessing breath" and so forth,
because of doubt regarding the self (ātman).
For this very reason, [the absence] from the counter-example (vipakṣa) must also be established;

for when a restriction (niyama) regarding one instance is proven, the exclusion of others is thereby established. Otherwise, even if non-existence were established for something seen in some cases, there would still remain doubt regarding that which is not seen.

For instance, some objects are observed to belong to a certain genus even though they do not pervade all individual instances of that genus, such as the property of being made of earth or being scratchable by iron.
Furthermore, because no contradiction is observed, there is only doubt;
for a contradiction between the absence of self (*nairātmya*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—characterized as stated above—is unestablished.
The exclusion [of breath and so forth] from selflessness is doubtful;

for if there were a specific determination of a self, then, by virtue of being the nature of its effect, breath and so forth would be contradictory to selflessness. And it has already been stated that this [determination] is not established.

Granted that there may indeed be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of breath and so forth with the absence of self, and that upon the presence of those [breaths], there is the exclusion of the absence of self;
nevertheless, it is not from the mere absence of "non-self" that the self is established in the living body,
such that this [absence] would not constitute a lack of negative concomitance.

4: He desires existence; for example, even in the absence of exclusion [from the dissimilar instance], the vital breaths and so forth are not accepted as being present in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
If a reason is not excluded from the similar instance, it is therefore a reason that possesses positive concomitance (*anvayin*).
"If it were not [the case that] there is no selfhood through positive and negative concomitance, then it would possess a self"—this is the summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka).
[Verse 5: There is no cognition of a self by means of the occurrence of breath and so forth, because that would exclude selflessness.
Rather, how then are the vital breaths and so forth established? Only by way of positive injunction.
